title: Prayers for others
hook: blessings for the sick, the community and the country

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah, the Prophets answering the Torah. Your line was comfort after the warning. Today, the prayers said around the open scroll, for other people.

While the Torah lies open on the table, there's a pause between readings. Someone walks up to the leader and whispers a name. Then another. Then a list on a scrap of paper. A neighbor's husband after surgery. A cousin's newborn. A friend in rehab. The leader starts a short prayer, and when it reaches the gap, the names pour in, sometimes for a full minute. In some congregations, people simply stand and say them aloud, one after another, until the room goes quiet again.
screen: `A NAME WHISPERED TO THE LEADER.` → `A LIST ON A SCRAP OF PAPER.` → `THE NAMES POUR IN.`

segments.voice: The prayer begins Mi sheberach avoteinu: may the One who blessed our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in many communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, bless this person. It's a frame, and almost anything can go in it. There's a Mi Sheberach for each person called up to the Torah. One for the sick, asking for complete healing of body and spirit, where the names from that scrap of paper go. One for the whole congregation and everyone who gives to it and serves it. One for a new baby, one for a couple about to marry. Many synagogues also pray for the country and its leaders, and in many communities for the State of Israel and those who defend it. Praying for the government has deep roots. The prophet Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, in the old Jewish translation: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Not Jerusalem, the city they lost. Babylon, the city that took them captive. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says to pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow one another alive. In recent decades the songwriter Debbie Friedman wrote a sung version of the prayer for healing, and some synagogues now sing it instead. The frame stays the same: the blessing that reached our ancestors, asked for someone else.
screen: `MAY THE ONE WHO BLESSED OUR ANCESTORS.` · `FOR THE SICK, THE CALLED UP, THE NEW.` · `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `PRAY FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S WELFARE.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you live: the main street, the school, the hospital, the people you pass without knowing their names, and the people who run it, the ones you voted for and the ones you didn't. Hold one wish for the whole place, safety, fairness, enough. If you pray, ask for its peace; if not, just let yourself care, for a minute, about people you'll never meet.
Mi Sheberach. May the One who blessed. The prayer said around the Torah for the sick, the congregation, and the country.
Your line: pray for the city. Even the city you didn't choose. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: During the Torah service, Mi Sheberach blessings are said for those called up, for the sick, whose names are added aloud or whispered to the leader, and for the congregation; many synagogues also say prayers for the country and for the State of Israel.

seek its peace and pray for it.
ignore it and keep to yourselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer for sick people.
what it means: a frame for blessing others, from the sick to the whole country, asking the ancestors' blessing for someone else.
what a scholar hears: Jeremiah 29:7; Pirkei Avot 3:2, Rabbi Chanina segan hakohanim; prayers for the government in medieval siddurim (Hanoten teshuah); Debbie Friedman's sung version.

chat.says: Why does the synagogue pray for the government? Isn't that a bit political?
options: It's an old practice: Jeremiah told exiles to pray for the peace of their city.
It's a newer custom that began with the founding of the modern State of Israel.
It's only said in Israel, for the Israeli government and its leaders.
chat.meaning: Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon, and Pirkei Avot says to pray for the government's welfare.

Mi Sheberach.meaning: may the One who blessed; a prayer for others

Pirkei Avot.meaning: a Mishnah tractate of the sages' sayings

Jeremiah.meaning: a prophet who wrote to the exiles in Babylon

Babylon.meaning: the empire that carried the people of Judah into exile

sources.ref: Mi Sheberach prayers in the Torah service

notes: Jeremiah 29:7 quoted as JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Pirkei Avot 3:2: Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests; paraphrased.
Debbie Friedman's Mi Shebeirach (written around 1987) is named but not quoted (it is under copyright).
Prayer for the State of Israel and its defenders is said in many but not all communities; described as 'in many communities'.
The tomorrow title 'Our duty to praise' (Aleinu) follows the outline.
